mainTopic: ראש השנה as the יום הדין, and the start of the year for שמיטה and יובל.
overview: This amud finishes the proof that ראש השנה is the day of judgment, from the פסוק "כִּי חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מִשְׁפָּט לֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב". Two ברייתות learn more from that פסוק. The first teaches that the בית דין של מעלה waits for the earthly בית דין to sanctify the month. The second teaches that אומות העולם are judged too, but ישראל goes first. The גמרא compares this to רב חסדא's rule that a king is judged before his people, and gives two reasons for that rule. Next the גמרא returns to the משנה and learns through a גזירה שוה of 'שנה' that שמיטה counts from תשרי, not ניסן. It then asks how יובל can start on the first of תשרי when its שופר is blown on יום הכיפורים. The answer is that the משנה follows רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא, who holds the יובל year is holy from ראש השנה, while the release of slaves and fields waits for יום הכיפורים. A final ברייתא teaches that this holiness ends with the fiftieth year and does not spill into the fifty-first.

steps.title: Completing the proof that the hidden-moon festival is the day of judgment
steps.stepSummary: The festival when the moon is hidden must be ראש השנה, and the next פסוק calls it a day of מִשְׁפָּט.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which festival falls when the moon is covered? You must say it is ראש השנה. And it is written right after: "For it is a statute for Israel, a judgment of the God of Jacob."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a proof that started on the previous amud. It identifies the "covered moon" festival as ראש השנה and shows from the next פסוק that this day is a day of judgment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier פסוק (בַּכֵּסֶה) points to a festival at the start of a month, when the moon cannot be seen. Only ראש השנה fits. The very next פסוק uses the word מִשְׁפָּט, so ראש השנה is the day of judgment.

keyTerms.meaning: is covered or hidden (the new moon is not visible)
you must say; the only possible answer is

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source that ראש השנה is the יום הדין. The rest of this passage builds on this same פסוק.

phrases.english: on which the moon is covered
phrases.notes: This finishes the question from before: which festival falls when the moon is hidden?

phrases.english: you must say this is Rosh HaShanah.
And it is written: "For it is a statute for Israel,"
phrases.notes: תהלים פ״א:ה׳, the very next פסוק.

phrases.english: a judgment of the God of Jacob."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the derivation earlier.
steps.raayaObject: That ראש השנה (in תשרי) is the day of judgment.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים פ״א:ד׳-ה׳: the "כֵּסֶה" festival followed by "מִשְׁפָּט לֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב".

steps.title: The heavenly court waits for the earthly court
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the פסוק that judgment in Heaven begins only after the earthly בית דין sanctifies the month.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: "For it is a statute for Israel, a judgment of the God of Jacob." This teaches that the heavenly court does not enter into judgment until the earthly court has sanctified the month.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that learns a new idea from the same פסוק. Heaven's judgment depends on when the בית דין below declares the new month.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק puts "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" (what Israel fixes) before "מִשְׁפָּט לֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב" (God's judgment). The ברייתא reads this order as a rule. First ישראל's court sets the day of ראש השנה, and only then does the heavenly court sit in judgment.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean Heaven cannot judge without people. It means Heaven chose to fix the date of judgment by the earthly court's declaration of the month.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how much authority קידוש החודש by בית דין has: even the heavenly calendar follows it.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: "For it is a statute for Israel,"
a judgment of the God of Jacob"

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁאֵין בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה נִכְנָסִין לַדִּין
phrases.english: this teaches that the heavenly court does not enter into judgment
unless the month has been sanctified

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה אֶת הַחֹדֶשׁ.
phrases.english: by the earthly court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the פסוק just cited and brings a ברייתא that learns a further lesson from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The heavenly judgment of ראש השנה begins only after the earthly בית דין sanctifies the month.

steps.title: Are the nations also judged on this day?
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא notes that "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" mentions only ישראל and asks where we learn that אומות העולם are judged too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא taught: "For it is a statute for Israel." From this I only know about Israel. From where do I know about the nations of the world?
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא begins with a question. The פסוק says "for Israel," so how do we know the rest of the world is judged on ראש השנה too? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" seem to limit the judgment to ישראל alone. The ברייתא asks for a source that expands the judgment to all nations.

phrases.english: Another baraita taught: "For it is a statute for Israel"
I have only Israel,
for the nations of the world, from where?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם מִנַּיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different ברייתא reads the same פסוק in another way.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that אומות העולם are also judged on ראש השנה.

steps.title: The God of Jacob judges the whole world
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the פסוק, "מִשְׁפָּט לֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב", includes the nations.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: "a judgment of the God of Jacob."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its question. The phrase "judgment of the God of Jacob" refers to God as Judge of everyone, so the nations are judged too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" speaks about ישראל. "מִשְׁפָּט לֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב" speaks about God's judgment in general, and God rules over the whole world. So this half of the פסוק includes all of humanity.

keyTerms.meaning: the verse teaches; therefore the פסוק says

phrases.english: The verse states: "a judgment of the God of Jacob."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "מִשְׁפָּט לֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב" includes אומות העולם in the judgment.

steps.title: Then why mention Israel specifically?
steps.stepSummary: If the second half already covers everyone, what does "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" add?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what does the verse teach by saying "For it is a statute for Israel"?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now asks why ישראל is named at all, since "judgment of the God of Jacob" already includes everyone. This sets up the next step's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words of a פסוק are not extra. Once the whole world is included, naming ישראל separately must teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: if so; if that is true
what does the verse come to teach?

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן, מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״כִּי חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל״,
phrases.english: If so, what does the verse teach with "For it is a statute for Israel"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the answer in step 4, which seems to make "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" unnecessary.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra lesson the words "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" teach.

steps.title: Israel enters judgment first
steps.stepSummary: Naming ישראל first teaches that ישראל is judged before the nations.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches that Israel enters into judgment first.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question. ישראל is mentioned first because ישראל is judged first on ראש השנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ישראל and אומות העולם are judged on ראש השנה. The extra words teach the order of the judgment, not who is judged.
steps.whatToRemember: On ראש השנה the whole world is judged, and ישראל goes in first.

phrases.english: This teaches that Israel enters into judgment first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל" teaches that ישראל is judged before the nations.

steps.title: Like רב חסדא: the king is judged before the people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא links "ישראל first" to רב חסדא's rule that a king is judged before his community.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like רב חסדא. For רב חסדא said: When a king and a community come for judgment, the king enters judgment first, as it says: "the judgment of His servant and the judgment of His people."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the idea of "who goes first in judgment" matches a statement of רב חסדא. A king is judged before his nation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In שלמה המלך's prayer (מלכים א ח:נט), "His servant" (the king) is mentioned before "His people." רב חסדא learns from this order that the leader is judged first. In the same way, ישראל, God's special nation, is judged before the other nations.

keyTerms.meaning: in line with the view of רב חסדא
the judgment of His servant (the king)
as it is said (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: The order of the words in a פסוק can teach the order of judgment. The king comes before the people, and ישראל comes before the nations.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a general principle about the order of judgment that supports the ברייתא's teaching.

phrases.english: In accordance with Rav Chisda. For Rav Chisda said:

phrases.aramaic: מֶלֶךְ וְצִיבּוּר — מֶלֶךְ נִכְנָס תְּחִילָּה לַדִּין,
phrases.english: A king and a community: the king enters judgment first,
as it is said: "the judgment of His servant and the judgment of His people."
phrases.notes: מלכים א ח:נט, from שלמה's prayer at the dedication of the בית המקדש.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 6's rule of order with a parallel principle from an אמורא.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that an order of priority exists in Divine judgment (ישראל first).
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב חסדא's derivation from "מִשְׁפַּט עַבְדּוֹ וּמִשְׁפַּט עַמּוֹ" that the king is judged before the people.

steps.title: Why is the king judged first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב חסדא's rule that the king is judged before his community.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the king should be judged before everyone else. This short question sets up the two answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 told us the rule: the king goes first. Now the גמרא wants to know why. This is a request for the logic, not an attack on the rule.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: Why is the king brought into judgment before the community?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רב חסדא's rule quoted in Step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the king is judged before his community.

steps.title: Two reasons the king goes first
steps.stepSummary: Reason one: it is not respectful to make a king wait outside. Reason two: he is judged before God's anger builds up from the community's sins.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: it is not proper for a king to stand outside and wait. Or if you want, say: he is judged first, before God's anger grows stronger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two different reasons why the king is judged first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason is about honor: a king should not be kept waiting outside while his people are judged. The second reason is for his own good: if he is judged first, he is judged before the community's sins stir up more Divine anger, so his judgment is gentler. 'אי בעית אימא' means both reasons are acceptable, and the גמרא does not choose between them.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say (introduces one possible answer)

steps.whatToRemember: ישראל is judged before אומות העולם, just as a king is judged before his people. This is either for honor or so that the judgment is kinder, before Divine anger builds up.
steps.confusionAlert: The two answers do not argue with each other about the rule. Both agree the king goes first. They only give different reasons for it.

phrases.english: If you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: לָאו אוֹרַח אַרְעָא לְמֵיקַם מַלְכָּא אַבָּרַאי,
phrases.english: it is not proper conduct for the king to stand outside,
phrases.notes: Waiting while his subjects are judged would be beneath his honor.

phrases.english: and if you wish, say:
before the anger grows stronger.
phrases.notes: The community's sins could increase Divine anger, so judging the king first protects him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Two reasons: the king's honor (he should not wait outside), or protection from Divine anger that grows stronger because of the community's sins.

steps.title: Source for שמיטה starting in תשרי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's next item, 'and for שמיטין', and asks for its source.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And for שמיטין.' From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה, which said the first of תשרי is the new year for שמיטה, and asks how we know that. It is setting up the source that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A new section begins here. The question is which day starts the counting of the שמיטה year. The גמרא wants a פסוק behind the משנה's claim that it is תשרי.

keyTerms.meaning: Sabbatical years (every seventh year, when the land rests)
From where do we know it?

phrases.english: And for Sabbatical Years.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה: the first of תשרי is the new year for these.

phrases.english: From where do we derive this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's list after finishing the topic of judgment.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source that the שמיטה year begins in תשרי.

steps.title: Learning 'שנה' from 'שנה'
steps.stepSummary: The שמיטה פסוק uses the word 'שנה', and we learn its meaning from 'מראשית השנה', which refers to a year that begins in תשרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And in the seventh year shall be a Sabbath of rest for the land.' And we learn 'year' from 'year' that it starts from תשרי, as it is written: 'From the beginning of the year.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a גזירה שוה: the word 'year' in the שמיטה פסוק is linked to the word 'year' in a פסוק that means a year beginning in תשרי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שמיטה פסוק does not tell us when the year starts. So the גמרא links it to 'מראשית השנה' (דברים יא), which describes the rainy-season year that begins in תשרי. Because the same word appears in both places, the meaning carries over: the שמיטה year also starts in תשרי.

keyTerms.meaning: We learn / derive (here, through a גזירה שוה)
Learning from a shared word that appears in two פסוקים
From the beginning of the year

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And in the seventh year'
'shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land,'
and we learn 'year' from 'year' that it is from Tishrei,
as it is written: 'From the beginning of the year.'
phrases.notes: דברים יא:יב. This refers to a year that begins with the rainy season, in תשרי.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״וּבַשָּׁנָה הַשְּׁבִיעִית שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן יִהְיֶה לָאָרֶץ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source requested in Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of 'שנה'–'שנה' from 'מראשית השנה', a year beginning in תשרי.

steps.title: Why not learn from ניסן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: why not link 'שנה' to the פסוק about ניסן, 'ראשון הוא לכם לחדשי השנה', and start שמיטה in ניסן?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us learn 'year' from 'year' from ניסן, as it is written: 'It shall be the first to you of the months of the year'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: the word 'year' also appears in a פסוק about ניסן, so maybe the שמיטה year should start in ניסן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה שוה needs the matching word, and 'שנה' appears in more than one place. If it also appears in a פסוק that points to ניסן, why choose the תשרי פסוק? This challenge attacks how the source in Step 11 picked its match.

keyTerms.meaning: Of the months of the year

phrases.english: But let us learn 'year' from 'year' from Nisan,
as it is written: 'It is first for you'
'of the months of the year'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the choice of a תשרי-linked פסוק for the גזירה שוה in Step 11.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'שנה' also appears in a פסוק about ניסן, so the same method could lead to ניסן instead.

steps.title: Match a 'year' without months to a 'year' without months
steps.stepSummary: The שמיטה פסוק says 'year' without mentioning months, like 'מראשית השנה'. The ניסן פסוק mentions months, so it is a weaker match.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn a 'year' that has no months mentioned with it from a 'year' that has no months mentioned with it. We do not learn a 'year' with no months from a 'year' that has months mentioned with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that we choose the closer match: both the שמיטה פסוק and 'מראשית השנה' say 'year' alone, while the ניסן פסוק talks about months.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When two פסוקים could be linked, we pick the one most similar in context. 'לחדשי השנה' is about counting months, which starts in ניסן. A plain 'year' with no months, like in שמיטה, matches the plain 'year' of 'מראשית השנה'. So the source from תשרי stands.

keyTerms.meaning: That has no months mentioned with it
That has months mentioned with it

steps.whatToRemember: שמיטה counts from תשרי because its 'year' (with no months mentioned) matches the תשרי-type 'year' of 'מראשית השנה', not the ניסן 'year' of months.

phrases.english: We derive a 'year' that has no months with it
from a 'year' that has no months with it,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין דָּנִין שָׁנָה שֶׁאֵין עִמָּהּ חֳדָשִׁים
phrases.english: and we do not derive a 'year' that has no months with it
from a 'year' that has months with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּנִין שָׁנָה שֶׁאֵין עִמָּהּ חֳדָשִׁים מִשָּׁנָה שֶׁאֵין עִמָּהּ חֳדָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12 and defends Step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Closer-context rule for choosing the matching word in a גזירה שוה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any appearance of 'שנה' could serve as the source, including the ניסן פסוק.
steps.terutzMaskana: We link 'שנה' with no months to 'שנה' with no months, so שמיטה starts in תשרי.

steps.title: Doesn't יובל begin on יום הכיפורים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'and for יובלות' from the משנה and challenges it: the יובל seems to begin on the tenth of תשרי, when the שופר is blown on יום הכיפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And for יובלות.' Is the יובל on the first of תשרי? The יובל is on the tenth of תשרי, as it is written: 'On יום הכיפורים you shall sound the שופר'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next item in the משנה, יובל, and challenges it. The Torah links the start of יובל to blowing the שופר on יום הכיפורים, which is the tenth of תשרי, not the first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the first of תשרי is the new year for יובלות. But the פסוק marks the יובל with the שופר on יום הכיפורים. That suggests the יובל year begins on the tenth, which seems to contradict the משנה. The answer comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the tenth of תשרי

phrases.english: And for Jubilee Years.
Is the Jubilee on the first of Tishrei?
The Jubilee is on the tenth of Tishrei,
as it is written: 'On Yom Kippur you shall sound the shofar'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next item in the משנה's list after finishing שמיטה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's statement that the first of תשרי is the new year for יובלות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah marks the יובל with the שופר on יום הכיפורים (the tenth of תשרי), which implies the יובל begins on the tenth, not the first.

steps.title: The משנה follows רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge: the משנה that starts יובל on ראש השנה follows רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא. He learns from a פסוק that the יובל year is holy from its very beginning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this? It is רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא, as a ברייתא teaches: Why does the פסוק say 'And you shall make holy the fiftieth year'? Since it says the שופר is blown 'on יום הכיפורים', I might think the year becomes holy only from יום הכיפורים onward. So the פסוק says 'And you shall make holy the fiftieth year', which teaches that the year is holy from its very beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 14 by naming the תנא behind the משנה. It brings a ברייתא showing that this תנא holds the יובל year is holy starting from ראש השנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge was that the שופר of יובל is blown on יום הכיפורים, so the year seemed to start on the 10th of תשרי. The ברייתא says the words 'make holy the fiftieth YEAR' refer to the whole year, so the holiness starts on ראש השנה. יום הכיפורים is only when the שופר is blown, not when the year begins.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose opinion is this? (a formula that names the author of an unnamed teaching)
The Jubilee, the fiftieth year, when slaves go free and fields return to their owners
One might think (introduces a possible but wrong idea)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the start of the year with the blowing of the שופר. According to this view, the יובל year starts on ראש השנה. The שופר on יום הכיפורים only triggers the release of slaves and the return of fields.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer saves the משנה's claim that ראש השנה (the 1st of תשרי) is the new year for יובלות.

phrases.english: Whose opinion is this?

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָא הִיא.
phrases.english: It is Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.
As it is taught in a baraita:
"And you shall make holy the fiftieth year"
Why does the verse need to say this?
Since it says "on Yom Kippur" (about blowing the shofar),
one might think the year does not become holy
except from Yom Kippur onward.
So the verse says: "And you shall make holy the fiftieth year,"
which teaches that it is holy from its very beginning onward.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מַנִּי — רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14 by naming the תנא of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Names the תנא: the משנה follows one specific opinion, which has a source in a פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the שופר is blown on יום הכיפורים, the יובל would begin on the 10th of תשרי.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא, the יובל is holy from ראש השנה, as the משנה says.

steps.title: The in-between days from ראש השנה to יום הכיפורים
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא describes what happens in practice. From ראש השנה to יום הכיפורים the slaves are neither sent home nor working for their masters. On יום הכיפורים the שופר is blown, and the release takes effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here רבי ישמעאל said: From ראש השנה until יום הכיפורים, slaves were not sent home, and they did not work for their masters. Instead, they ate, drank, and celebrated with crowns on their heads. When יום הכיפורים came, בית דין blew the שופר, slaves went home, and fields returned to their owners.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל spells out what his view means in real life. For ten days, the slaves live in a halfway state, already free from work but not yet sent home.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the year is already holy from ראש השנה, the masters can no longer make the slaves work. But the actual release only happens with the שופר on יום הכיפורים. So the slaves spend those days celebrating like free people.

keyTerms.meaning: From here (introduces a practical result of what was just learned)
Their crowns (a sign of freedom and joy)
Fields return to their original owners

steps.whatToRemember: In יובל, the holiness of the year starts on ראש השנה. The release of slaves and the return of fields happen on יום הכיפורים, when the שופר is blown.

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן אָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָא:
phrases.english: From here Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, said:
From Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur
slaves were not released to their homes,
and they were not working for their masters.
Rather, they ate, drank, and rejoiced,
with their crowns on their heads.
Once Yom Kippur arrived,
the court blew the shofar,
slaves were released to their homes,
and fields returned to their owners.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכָּאן אָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical result of the ברייתא in Step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From ראש השנה to יום הכיפורים of יובל, slaves stop working but are not yet released. On יום הכיפורים the שופר frees them and returns the fields.

steps.title: How do the רבנן use this פסוק?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the רבנן, who disagree with רבי ישמעאל: what do they learn from 'וקדשתם את שנת החמשים'?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? (How do they explain this פסוק?)
steps.whatsHappening: With one word, the גמרא asks what the רבנן do with the פסוק that רבי ישמעאל used. This sets up the next step, where the answer comes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן do not agree that the יובל is holy from ראש השנה. Still, every word of the תורה must teach something, so the גמרא asks what this פסוק teaches them.

keyTerms.meaning: And the Sages (asking: how do they deal with this?)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis? (What do they learn from this verse?)
phrases.notes: The גמרא only says 'and the Rabbis?' and leaves the rest of the question for us to fill in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from רבי ישמעאל's reading to the opposing view's use of the same פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from 'וקדשתם את שנת החמשים', since they don't use it to start יובל on ראש השנה.

steps.title: Years are sanctified, but not months
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn from the פסוק that בית דין formally declares the יובל year holy. There is no such declaration for months.
steps.simpleTranslation: Years you make holy, but months you do not make holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן use the פסוק for a different lesson. It teaches that בית דין sanctifies the year of יובל, but does not sanctify months in this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן read 'make holy the fiftieth YEAR' as a מצוה to formally declare the year holy. The word 'year' limits this to years, so months get no such declaration. Since the פסוק is used for this lesson, it no longer proves that יובל starts on ראש השנה.

phrases.english: Years you sanctify,
but you do not sanctify months.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנִים אַתָּה מְקַדֵּשׁ, וְאִי אַתָּה מְקַדֵּשׁ חֳדָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן learn from the פסוק that בית דין formally sanctifies the יובל year, but not months.

steps.title: Another ברייתא: maybe the יובל's holiness extends past its end
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא asks why the פסוק says 'יובל היא'. It suggests that just as holiness starts at the beginning of the year, it might also continue past the end, since we usually add extra time to holy days.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: Why does the פסוק say 'It is a יובל'? Since it says 'And you shall make holy the fiftieth year', I might think that just as the year is holy from its beginning, it also stays holy past its end. And don't be surprised at this idea, since we do add ordinary time onto holy time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that sets up a possible mistaken idea. Maybe the holiness of יובל spills over into the next year, until יום הכיפורים of year 51. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is a mirror image: if יובל started ten days before the שופר, maybe it also lasts until יום הכיפורים of the next year. This idea is reasonable because of תוספת מחול על קודש, which adds ordinary time onto holy days like שבת and יום טוב.

keyTerms.meaning: We add ordinary time onto holy time

phrases.english: Another baraita teaches:
"It is a Jubilee": why does the verse say this?
Since it says: "And you shall make holy the fiftieth year,"
one might think that just as it is holy from its beginning onward,
so too it stays holy past its end.
And do not be surprised at this idea,
for we do add ordinary time onto holy time.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: ״יוֹבֵל הִיא״ — מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 15's idea that holiness starts early, and asks whether it also extends later.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up a possible idea: the יובל's holiness might continue into the 51st year, based on תוספת מחול על קודש.

steps.title: Only the fiftieth year is holy, not the fifty-first
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'יובל היא שנת החמשים' limits the holiness to year 50 alone. None of it carries into year 51.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the פסוק says: 'It is a יובל, the fiftieth year.' You make the fiftieth year holy, but you do not make the fifty-first year holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא rejects the idea from the last step. The words 'It is... the fiftieth year' show that the holiness stops when year 50 ends.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reads 'יובל היא שנת החמשים' as defining the יובל as the fiftieth year itself: 'the fiftieth year you sanctify, but not the fifty-first.' So even though the יובל starts early (on ראש השנה, before the שופר), it does not run late into year 51. The usual rule of adding ordinary time onto holy time does not apply at the end of יובל.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי ישמעאל, the יובל is holy from ראש השנה of year 50, and its release happens on יום הכיפורים. Its holiness ends with year 50 and does not continue into year 51.

phrases.english: So the verse says: "It is a Jubilee, the fiftieth year":
the fiftieth year you sanctify,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אַתָּה מְקַדֵּשׁ שְׁנַת הַחֲמִשִּׁים וְאַחַת.
phrases.english: but you do not sanctify the fifty-first year.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the possible idea raised in Step 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The holiness of יובל covers only the fiftieth year. It does not extend into the fifty-first year.
